title: Phishing Email Under Pressure
description: Spot social-engineering warning signs and respond safely to an urgent account-verification email.
learningOutcome: Recognise phishing indicators, verify requests through trusted channels and report suspicious messages.

steps.situation: An email says your work account will be suspended in ten minutes unless you verify it.
steps.question: What should you examine first?

choices.text: Only the company logo and colours
choices.feedback: Branding can be copied. Check the sender, link and context as well.

choices.text: The sender address, destination link and whether the request was expected
choices.feedback: Correct. Independent checks are more reliable than the message's appearance or urgency.

choices.text: Click immediately because the message is urgent
choices.feedback: Urgency is a common social-engineering tactic and should not replace verification.

choices.text: Ask a manager whether the message looks official before inspecting the technical details
choices.feedback: A second opinion may help, but sender, link and context checks are still required.

steps.situation: The visible link says company-login.com, but hovering shows company-login-security.net.
steps.question: What is the safest action?

choices.text: Open it in a private browser window
choices.feedback: Private mode does not make a malicious website safe.

choices.text: Forward it to a colleague to test
choices.feedback: Forwarding can spread the threat to other users.

choices.text: Copy the destination into a search engine to see whether the site appears in results
choices.feedback: Search results do not prove that a login page is legitimate or safe.

choices.text: Do not click; open the official service separately and report the message
choices.feedback: Correct. Use a known route and report the suspicious domain.

steps.situation: The email asks for your password and multi-factor authentication code.
steps.question: How should you respond?

choices.text: Refuse, close the message and contact IT through the official support channel
choices.feedback: Correct. Legitimate support should not request your password or one-time code by email.

choices.text: Send only the password but keep the code private
choices.feedback: A password alone can still compromise the account.

choices.text: Reply asking whether the request is genuine
choices.feedback: Replying keeps you inside the suspicious channel; verify independently instead.

choices.text: Use a separate device to send the requested verification code
choices.feedback: Changing devices does not make credential sharing safe.

steps.situation: You accidentally clicked the link but did not enter any details.
steps.question: What should you do next?

choices.text: Ignore it because no password was entered
choices.feedback: The visit may still matter; report it so the risk can be assessed.

choices.text: Refresh the page to check whether it looks real
choices.feedback: Repeated interaction increases exposure and provides no reliable verification.

choices.text: Close the page, report it and follow the organisation's security guidance
choices.feedback: Correct. Reporting allows the security team to assess the exposure quickly.

choices.text: Disconnect the device from the network but do not report the click
choices.feedback: Limiting exposure can help, but the security team still needs an accurate report.

steps.situation: A colleague says they received the same message.
steps.question: What is the best team response?

choices.text: Ask everyone to delete it quietly
choices.feedback: Deletion helps locally, but central reporting is still needed.

choices.text: Tell them not to interact with it and ensure the message is reported centrally
choices.feedback: Correct. A coordinated report helps protect other users.

choices.text: Post the link in the group chat as a warning
choices.feedback: Sharing the live link can cause accidental clicks.

choices.text: Take a screenshot and circulate the live message to every colleague
choices.feedback: A screenshot may support reporting, but broad circulation can spread confusion and risk.

title: Password Reset Impersonation
description: Handle a fake support call requesting credentials and remote access.
learningOutcome: Protect credentials and verify identity before taking account-related actions.

steps.situation: A caller claims to be IT support and says your password must be reset immediately.
steps.question: What should you do first?

choices.text: Ask the caller to confirm your employee number
choices.feedback: A criminal may already know basic details. Use an official channel.

choices.text: Follow the instructions because the caller sounds professional
choices.feedback: Tone and confidence do not prove identity.

choices.text: End the call and contact IT using the official number or portal
choices.feedback: Correct. Independent verification prevents impersonation fraud.

choices.text: Keep the caller on the line while checking their name in the staff directory
choices.feedback: A directory entry does not verify that the caller is the person they claim to be.

steps.situation: The caller asks you to install a remote-access tool.
steps.question: What is the safest response?

choices.text: Refuse and report the request to IT or security
choices.feedback: Correct. Unapproved remote access can expose the whole device.

choices.text: Install it but close confidential files first
choices.feedback: Remote access can still expose credentials and systems.

choices.text: Ask the caller to email the link
choices.feedback: An email link from an unverified person is not safer.

choices.text: Install the tool temporarily and remove it after the reset
choices.feedback: Even brief unapproved remote access can expose credentials and systems.

steps.situation: You receive a password-reset link moments after the call.
steps.question: How should you handle it?

choices.text: Use the link because it arrived from an automated address
choices.feedback: Sender names and automated templates can be spoofed.

choices.text: Forward it to your personal email to check later
choices.feedback: This moves potentially malicious content outside company controls.

choices.text: Scan the link with normal antivirus software and use it if no alert appears
choices.feedback: A clean scan is not proof that the link or reset process is genuine.

choices.text: Use the official account portal instead of the link and report the sequence of events
choices.feedback: Correct. The combination of call and email is a strong warning sign.

steps.situation: The caller knows your manager's name and current project.
steps.question: Does this prove they are genuine?

choices.text: Yes; outsiders would not know those details
choices.feedback: Attackers often research targets before contacting them.

choices.text: No; public or leaked information can be used to sound convincing
choices.feedback: Correct. Verify identity through official processes.

choices.text: Probably, but share only part of the password
choices.feedback: Passwords should never be shared, even partially.

choices.text: Ask a personal question about your manager before deciding
choices.feedback: Attackers may research personal details; official verification is still necessary.

steps.situation: You already provided your username but no password.
steps.question: What should you do?

choices.text: Do nothing because usernames are always public
choices.feedback: The information may be useful for follow-up attacks and should be reported.

choices.text: Call the number back and demand deletion
choices.feedback: Re-engaging through the suspicious number can increase risk.

choices.text: Report it promptly and follow the official account-protection steps
choices.feedback: Correct. Early reporting can prevent further targeting.

choices.text: Change the password through the official portal but do not report the contact
choices.feedback: Using the official portal is sensible, but reporting helps stop follow-up attacks against others.

title: Slip Hazard in a Busy Area
description: Respond to a spill safely while keeping people moving and recording the hazard.
learningOutcome: Control an immediate hazard, communicate clearly and complete the correct reporting process.

steps.situation: You notice water on a polished floor near a busy doorway.
steps.question: What is the first priority?

choices.text: Take a photo before doing anything
choices.feedback: Evidence may help later, but first prevent someone from slipping.

choices.text: Wait for housekeeping to notice it
choices.feedback: Leaving the hazard uncontrolled exposes others to injury.

choices.text: Ask a nearby colleague to watch the area while you continue your other duties
choices.feedback: Temporary supervision helps, but the area still needs a proper barrier and cleaning response.

choices.text: Prevent access to the area and place a warning sign while arranging cleaning
choices.feedback: Correct. Control the immediate risk before anything else.

steps.situation: No warning sign is immediately available.
steps.question: What should you do?

choices.text: Leave to search the whole building for a sign
choices.feedback: The hazard would be left unattended.

choices.text: Stand nearby or use a safe temporary barrier while requesting equipment
choices.feedback: Correct. Maintain control until proper equipment arrives.

choices.text: Cover the spill with paper towels and walk away
choices.feedback: Loose materials may create another hazard and the area remains unsafe.

choices.text: Place a chair near the spill and leave to find equipment
choices.feedback: An improvised marker may be missed and should not be left unmonitored.

steps.situation: A visitor tries to walk through the controlled area.
steps.question: How should you respond?

choices.text: Shout at them to stop
choices.feedback: The goal is safety without unnecessary escalation.

choices.text: Let them decide because the spill is small
choices.feedback: The risk must be controlled consistently.

choices.text: Politely explain the risk and direct them through a safe alternative route
choices.feedback: Correct. Clear, calm direction protects the visitor and keeps movement orderly.

choices.text: Tell the visitor to step over the spill carefully
choices.feedback: People should be redirected away from the hazard rather than encouraged through it.

steps.situation: The spill has been cleaned.
steps.question: What should happen before reopening the area?

choices.text: Confirm the surface is dry and remove barriers only when it is safe
choices.feedback: Correct. Visual cleanliness does not always mean the surface is safe.

choices.text: Remove the sign as soon as mopping finishes
choices.feedback: The floor may still be wet and slippery.

choices.text: Leave all barriers in place for the rest of the day
choices.feedback: Controls should remain only as long as needed and should not create obstruction.

choices.text: Test the surface with your shoe before removing the barrier
choices.feedback: An informal test is unreliable; confirm the surface is properly dry and safe.

steps.situation: The same leak has happened twice this week.
steps.question: What is the best follow-up?

choices.text: Keep cleaning it whenever it appears
choices.feedback: Cleaning controls the symptom but not the cause.

choices.text: Stop reporting it because staff already know
choices.feedback: A clear record helps management prioritise a permanent fix.

choices.text: Leave a permanent warning sign but do not report the source of the leak
choices.feedback: The immediate warning matters, but repeated hazards also need investigation and repair.

choices.text: Record the repeated issue and escalate it for investigation and repair
choices.feedback: Correct. Repeated hazards require a root-cause response.

title: Customer Personal Data Request
description: Verify identity and handle a request for personal information without exposing customer data.
learningOutcome: Apply identity verification, data minimisation and secure communication principles.

steps.situation: A customer calls asking for a copy of all information held about them.
steps.question: What should you do first?

choices.text: Follow the approved identity-verification and data-request process
choices.feedback: Correct. Privacy requests must be handled through a controlled process.

choices.text: Read the information aloud because they know the account name
choices.feedback: Knowing a name does not prove identity.

choices.text: Ask them to send a social-media message
choices.feedback: Personal data should not be moved to an unapproved channel.

choices.text: Ask the customer to send identification to your personal email address
choices.feedback: Personal email is not an approved route for handling identity evidence.

steps.situation: The caller cannot complete the required security checks.
steps.question: What is the correct response?

choices.text: Give only the last few records
choices.feedback: Partial disclosure is still a privacy breach.

choices.text: Use your judgement if they sound upset
choices.feedback: Empathy matters, but it does not replace verification.

choices.text: Do not disclose data; explain the approved alternative verification route
choices.feedback: Correct. Be helpful without weakening the control.

choices.text: Arrange a callback using verified account contact details and follow the formal process
choices.feedback: A verified callback may support the process, but disclosure must still follow approved controls.

steps.situation: The request includes another person's information.
steps.question: What should you do?

choices.text: Send everything because it is stored in the same account
choices.feedback: Storage location does not remove another person's privacy rights.

choices.text: Separate the information and escalate for privacy review before release
choices.feedback: Correct. Third-party data must be protected.

choices.text: Delete the other person's records
choices.feedback: Records should not be altered without authority.

choices.text: Redact the other person's name yourself and send the remaining file without review
choices.feedback: Informal redaction can miss identifiers and still requires an authorised privacy review.

steps.situation: You are ready to send the approved information.
steps.question: Which delivery method is best?

choices.text: Attach it to a normal email without protection
choices.feedback: Standard email may not provide sufficient protection.

choices.text: Upload it to a public file-sharing link
choices.feedback: Public links can expose data to unauthorised access.

choices.text: Send a password-protected file and put the password in the same email
choices.feedback: Sending the password in the same channel weakens the protection.

choices.text: Use the organisation's approved secure delivery method
choices.feedback: Correct. Sensitive data should be protected in transit.

steps.situation: The customer asks why the process takes time.
steps.question: How should you explain it?

choices.text: Explain that verification and review protect their privacy and ensure accuracy
choices.feedback: Correct. Transparent communication builds trust without revealing internal security details.

choices.text: Say the organisation does not trust customers
choices.feedback: That is inaccurate and unnecessarily confrontational.

choices.text: Promise immediate release regardless of checks
choices.feedback: You should not bypass required controls or make an unsafe promise.

choices.text: Explain the process but reveal the approximate number of records before verification
choices.feedback: The explanation is useful, but details about held data should wait until identity is verified.

title: Suspicious Bag at an Event Entrance
description: Manage an unattended item near a busy entrance using distance, communication and controlled escalation.
learningOutcome: Establish a safe boundary, provide accurate information and support a coordinated response.

steps.situation: A visitor reports an unattended backpack beside the entrance queue.
steps.question: What should you do first?

choices.text: Move it behind the barrier yourself
choices.feedback: Handling an unknown item creates unnecessary risk.

choices.text: Keep people away, avoid touching it and notify the control room
choices.feedback: Correct. Distance and escalation are the safest immediate actions.

choices.text: Wait to see whether someone claims it
choices.feedback: Waiting without controlling the area exposes more people.

choices.text: Move closer and photograph the bag before contacting control
choices.feedback: Approaching an unidentified item increases risk and is unnecessary for the initial report.

steps.situation: The control room asks for details.
steps.question: Which information is most useful?

choices.text: Your guess about what is inside
choices.feedback: Assumptions are less useful than precise observations.

choices.text: Only say that there is a bag
choices.feedback: This starts the report but lacks important detail.

choices.text: Provide the location and appearance but add a guess about what may be inside
choices.feedback: Useful facts should be separated from speculation.

choices.text: Exact location, appearance, nearby activity and time first noticed
choices.feedback: Correct. Observable facts support a proportionate response.

steps.situation: The queue is building as the area is redirected.
steps.question: How should you communicate with visitors?

choices.text: Give calm, simple directions without speculating about the threat
choices.feedback: Correct. Clear direction maintains safety and reduces panic.

choices.text: Tell everyone there may be a bomb
choices.feedback: Unverified claims can cause panic and disorder.

choices.text: Say nothing and physically block the route
choices.feedback: A barrier helps, but people also need clear direction.

choices.text: Explain that an operational issue requires a short diversion and give a clear alternative route
choices.feedback: This is calm and practical, although communication should remain aligned with the control team.

steps.situation: A person says the bag is theirs and tries to retrieve it.
steps.question: What is the best response?

choices.text: Let them collect it if they describe the colour
choices.feedback: A description alone is not enough to end the safety response.

choices.text: Ask them to open it in front of you
choices.feedback: Opening an unknown item is unsafe.

choices.text: Prevent access and pass the claim to the response lead for verification
choices.feedback: Correct. The controlled process should continue until authorised staff decide otherwise.

choices.text: Ask the claimant to wait beside the bag while you contact a supervisor
choices.feedback: The person should also be kept outside the controlled area.

steps.situation: Specialist support arrives.
steps.question: What should you do?

choices.text: Continue directing the incident independently
choices.feedback: Once responsibility is transferred, avoid conflicting instructions.

choices.text: Give a concise handover and follow the lead responder's instructions
choices.feedback: Correct. A clear handover supports coordinated command.

choices.text: Leave without giving any information
choices.feedback: The response team needs the facts you collected.

choices.text: Give the responder a description but omit when and where it was first noticed
choices.feedback: A description helps, but time and exact location are important parts of the handover.

title: Fire Alarm and Evacuation
description: Prioritise safe evacuation, accessibility support and accountability during a live alarm.
learningOutcome: Support an orderly evacuation and communicate critical information at the assembly point.

steps.situation: The fire alarm activates while the building is busy.
steps.question: What is your immediate priority?

choices.text: Search for visible fire before acting
choices.feedback: Delaying evacuation can increase harm.

choices.text: Wait for someone else to move first
choices.feedback: Staff should act promptly according to procedure.

choices.text: Begin the approved evacuation procedure and direct people to safe exits
choices.feedback: Correct. Life safety and orderly evacuation come first.

choices.text: Call a colleague to ask whether the alarm is a planned test before moving people
choices.feedback: Treat alarms as genuine unless an authorised process confirms otherwise.

steps.situation: A visitor wants to use the lift because they are on an upper floor.
steps.question: What should you do?

choices.text: Direct them to the approved evacuation route and arrange accessibility support
choices.feedback: Correct. Use the designated procedure and support plan.

choices.text: Allow the lift because it is faster
choices.feedback: Lifts may become unsafe during a fire incident.

choices.text: Tell them to remain alone until the alarm stops
choices.feedback: They need active support through the approved process.

choices.text: Use the lift only for the visitor with mobility needs because the stairs are difficult
choices.feedback: Accessibility support must follow the approved evacuation plan rather than an improvised lift decision.

steps.situation: Smoke is reported near one exit route.
steps.question: How should this affect your actions?

choices.text: Continue using the route until smoke is visible to you
choices.feedback: A credible report should be acted upon immediately.

choices.text: Open nearby doors to investigate
choices.feedback: Investigation may increase exposure and is not your first priority.

choices.text: Open the nearby door briefly to check how much smoke is present
choices.feedback: Opening doors can increase exposure and should not replace route control and reporting.

choices.text: Redirect people to the approved alternative route and inform control
choices.feedback: Correct. Avoid the affected route and update the incident picture.

steps.situation: At the assembly point, a person says their colleague may still be inside.
steps.question: What is the correct response?

choices.text: Go inside alone to search
choices.feedback: Unplanned re-entry may create another casualty.

choices.text: Pass the information to the emergency lead and prevent unplanned re-entry
choices.feedback: Correct. Trained responders need the information; re-entry creates more risk.

choices.text: Ignore it because the alarm could be false
choices.feedback: Missing-person information must be escalated.

choices.text: Send one trained colleague inside without telling the emergency lead
choices.feedback: Any search or rescue action must be coordinated by the authorised emergency command.

steps.situation: The alarm stops before an authorised all-clear is given.
steps.question: What should people do?

choices.text: Return immediately because the alarm is silent
choices.feedback: The hazard may still be present.

choices.text: Let each person decide
choices.feedback: Re-entry should be controlled and authorised.

choices.text: Remain at the assembly point until the authorised all-clear
choices.feedback: Correct. The end of the sound is not automatically permission to re-enter.

choices.text: Re-enter briefly to collect belongings because the alarm has stopped
choices.feedback: No one should re-enter before the authorised all-clear.

title: Aggressive Customer De-escalation
description: Use calm communication, safe positioning and proportionate escalation during a heated complaint.
learningOutcome: Reduce tension while protecting personal safety and maintaining professional boundaries.

steps.situation: A customer approaches shouting about a delayed service.
steps.question: What is the best opening response?

choices.text: Match their volume so they know you are serious
choices.feedback: Matching aggression usually escalates the interaction.

choices.text: Ignore them until they become quiet
choices.feedback: Silence may feel dismissive and increase frustration.

choices.text: State the rules immediately without first acknowledging the customer's concern
choices.feedback: Clear rules matter, but acknowledgement and calm listening reduce escalation.

choices.text: Use a calm tone, acknowledge the concern and invite them to explain
choices.feedback: Correct. Calm acknowledgement can reduce the need to shout for attention.

steps.situation: The customer moves closer and points at you.
steps.question: What should you do?

choices.text: Push their hand away
choices.feedback: Physical contact can escalate the incident.

choices.text: Maintain safe space, keep an exit route and set a calm boundary
choices.feedback: Correct. Position and boundaries support safety without provocation.

choices.text: Stand completely still even if blocked in
choices.feedback: You should preserve a safe route and request support if needed.

choices.text: Step sideways to maintain space and discreetly signal a colleague for support
choices.feedback: This improves safety and support, while calm boundaries should still be communicated.

steps.situation: They demand a promise you cannot authorise.
steps.question: How should you respond?

choices.text: Promise anything to end the argument
choices.feedback: A false promise can create a larger dispute later.

choices.text: Tell them there is absolutely nothing anyone can do
choices.feedback: That may be inaccurate and unnecessarily final.

choices.text: Explain what you can do, avoid false promises and offer the correct escalation route
choices.feedback: Correct. Clear options are more useful than an impossible promise.

choices.text: Transfer the customer to a manager without explaining what will happen next
choices.feedback: Escalation can help, but an unexplained handover may increase frustration.

steps.situation: The customer begins making threats.
steps.question: What is the appropriate next step?

choices.text: Prioritise safety, disengage where possible and request support according to procedure
choices.feedback: Correct. Threats change the risk level and require escalation.

choices.text: Challenge them to repeat the threat
choices.feedback: This may provoke further aggression.

choices.text: Continue the same conversation as if nothing changed
choices.feedback: The risk has changed and should be managed accordingly.

choices.text: Repeat a formal warning while continuing to manage the threat alone
choices.feedback: Once threats begin, personal safety and support should take priority.

steps.situation: The customer leaves and the immediate risk has ended.
steps.question: What should happen next?

choices.text: Post about the customer on social media
choices.feedback: That risks privacy, professionalism and evidence integrity.

choices.text: Only discuss it informally with colleagues
choices.feedback: Informal discussion does not replace official reporting.

choices.text: Record your opinion of the customer's attitude together with the factual details
choices.feedback: Incident records should remain objective and evidence-based.

choices.text: Record factual details and report through the approved incident process
choices.feedback: Correct. Accurate reporting supports follow-up and learning.

title: Crowd Pressure at an Entrance
description: Identify early crowd-pressure signs and coordinate safe flow before conditions become critical.
learningOutcome: Monitor density, communicate changes and protect escape routes during rising crowd pressure.

steps.situation: People are arriving faster than screening can process them.
steps.question: What is the best early action?

choices.text: Report the build-up, slow inflow and open the approved contingency plan
choices.feedback: Correct. Early intervention prevents pressure from becoming dangerous.

choices.text: Wait until the queue becomes physically unstable
choices.feedback: By then, options are more limited and risk is higher.

choices.text: Tell staff to work faster without changing flow
choices.feedback: Speed may help, but flow and capacity must be managed safely.

choices.text: Close the entrance immediately without coordinating with exits or control
choices.feedback: An uncoordinated closure can move pressure to another unsafe location.

steps.situation: The front of the queue is compressed against a barrier.
steps.question: What should you prioritise?

choices.text: Add another barrier to keep the line straight
choices.feedback: More rigid containment can increase compression.

choices.text: Ask people at the back to stop pushing by shouting
choices.feedback: Communication helps, but flow changes and team coordination are also needed.

choices.text: Reduce pressure, create space and coordinate controlled movement
choices.feedback: Correct. Relieving compression is the immediate safety priority.

choices.text: Remove the nearest barrier quickly without a controlled movement plan
choices.feedback: Sudden barrier changes can release pressure unpredictably.

steps.situation: One exit route has become partially blocked by equipment.
steps.question: What should happen?

choices.text: Leave it because the exit is not currently being used
choices.feedback: Emergency routes must be protected before they are needed.

choices.text: Keep the route clear immediately and report the obstruction
choices.feedback: Correct. Escape and relief routes must remain available.

choices.text: Move people closer to the equipment to create another lane
choices.feedback: This can worsen obstruction and trip risk.

choices.text: Ask the equipment owner to move it later after the busiest period
choices.feedback: Emergency routes must remain clear at all times.

steps.situation: A rumour spreads that the entrance is closing.
steps.question: How should staff respond?

choices.text: Repeat the rumour so people prepare
choices.feedback: Unverified information can trigger dangerous behaviour.

choices.text: Give different answers to different sections
choices.feedback: Conflicting messages undermine control.

choices.text: Give the crowd an estimated reopening time even though it has not been confirmed
choices.feedback: Unverified timing can damage trust and trigger further movement.

choices.text: Give consistent verified information and avoid contradicting messages
choices.feedback: Correct. Consistent communication reduces sudden movement and panic.

steps.situation: The area is stabilised.
steps.question: What is the best final action?

choices.text: Maintain monitoring, document the trigger and review the flow plan
choices.feedback: Correct. Stabilisation should be followed by learning and continued observation.

choices.text: Return immediately to normal capacity
choices.feedback: Conditions should be increased carefully and monitored.

choices.text: Delete the incident record because nobody was injured
choices.feedback: Near misses provide valuable prevention evidence.

choices.text: Increase capacity gradually once calm returns but do not record what caused the pressure
choices.feedback: A measured restart may be appropriate, but monitoring and learning must continue.

title: Ransomware Incident Containment
description: Coordinate technical and business decisions during a fast-moving ransomware event.
learningOutcome: Contain affected systems, preserve evidence and support controlled recovery decisions.

steps.situation: Multiple users report encrypted files and a ransom message.
steps.question: What should the response team prioritise first?

choices.text: Pay the ransom immediately to save time
choices.feedback: Payment does not guarantee recovery and should not bypass governance or legal review.

choices.text: Activate the incident plan, isolate affected systems and preserve evidence
choices.feedback: Correct. Rapid containment and structured command limit spread and support investigation.

choices.text: Restart every affected device
choices.feedback: Restarting may destroy volatile evidence or worsen recovery options.

choices.text: Shut down the entire network immediately without coordinating operational dependencies
choices.feedback: Isolation may be necessary, but uncontrolled shutdown can damage critical services and evidence.

steps.situation: The infection may be spreading through shared storage.
steps.question: What is the best next action?

choices.text: Ask users to keep working while monitoring
choices.feedback: Continued use may increase encryption and data loss.

choices.text: Delete all shared folders
choices.feedback: Destructive action can remove evidence and healthy data.

choices.text: Block every internet connection, including protected emergency communications
choices.feedback: Containment should be targeted and coordinated so essential communications remain available.

choices.text: Restrict affected network connections and coordinate isolation with IT operations
choices.feedback: Correct. Controlled isolation reduces spread while protecting critical services.

steps.situation: Senior management asks for a public statement within minutes.
steps.question: What should the response lead do?

choices.text: Provide verified facts, known impact, actions underway and clear uncertainty
choices.feedback: Correct. Fast communication should still be accurate and controlled.

choices.text: Announce that all data is safe before investigation
choices.feedback: Unsupported reassurance can damage trust and create legal risk.

choices.text: Refuse to communicate until the incident is completely resolved
choices.feedback: Silence may create confusion; provide carefully verified updates.

choices.text: Draft a public statement using the worst-case impact so it cannot underestimate the incident
choices.feedback: Public information must be based on verified facts and clearly stated uncertainty.

steps.situation: Backups exist, but their integrity is not yet confirmed.
steps.question: What is the safest recovery decision?

choices.text: Restore the newest backup immediately
choices.feedback: Recency does not guarantee integrity.

choices.text: Connect backup systems directly to the infected network
choices.feedback: This may expose the remaining recovery assets.

choices.text: Validate clean backups and recovery environments before restoration
choices.feedback: Correct. Restoring compromised backups can reintroduce the incident.

choices.text: Test restoration in an isolated environment while preserving the original backups
choices.feedback: This is a strong recovery control, alongside formal validation and approval.

steps.situation: The immediate threat is contained.
steps.question: What should happen before normal service resumes?

choices.text: Resume every service at once to reduce downtime
choices.feedback: A phased, tested recovery is safer.

choices.text: Confirm eradication, test recovery, monitor closely and record lessons learned
choices.feedback: Correct. Controlled recovery and review reduce repeat compromise.

choices.text: Close the incident because encryption has stopped
choices.feedback: Containment is not the same as full recovery.

choices.text: Reset all passwords and close the incident without extended monitoring
choices.feedback: Credential resets may help, but eradication, testing and monitoring are still required.

title: Major Incident Command Centre
description: Manage competing priorities, incomplete information and multi-team coordination during a major public incident.
learningOutcome: Establish command, maintain a shared operating picture and allocate resources by risk.

steps.situation: Reports of injuries, blocked access and crowd movement arrive at the same time.
steps.question: What should the incident lead establish first?

choices.text: Solve each message personally in the order received
choices.feedback: This creates overload and ignores relative risk.

choices.text: Wait for perfect information before assigning tasks
choices.feedback: Major incidents require action while information is still developing.

choices.text: A clear command structure, communication channel and immediate priorities
choices.feedback: Correct. Shared command prevents duplicated or conflicting action.

choices.text: Nominate separate team leads but allow each to keep a different incident log
choices.feedback: Delegated leadership helps, but a shared operating picture and log are essential.

steps.situation: Two teams give conflicting reports about the safest access route.
steps.question: How should this be handled?

choices.text: Verify through trusted sources, mark uncertainty and issue one coordinated instruction
choices.feedback: Correct. A shared operating picture should distinguish fact from uncertainty.

choices.text: Allow each team to use its preferred route
choices.feedback: Conflicting movement can increase congestion and risk.

choices.text: Choose the first report without checking
choices.feedback: Speed matters, but the decision should use the best available evidence.

choices.text: Combine both route reports and use the average estimated travel time
choices.feedback: Conflicting safety information must be verified, not averaged.

steps.situation: Media posts are spreading unverified casualty numbers.
steps.question: What is the best communication response?

choices.text: Repeat the highest number so the public takes it seriously
choices.feedback: Unverified figures can cause panic and damage credibility.

choices.text: Ask all staff to respond individually online
choices.feedback: Multiple unofficial voices create contradiction and disclosure risks.

choices.text: Pause all public updates until every detail has been confirmed
choices.feedback: Silence can create an information vacuum; verified updates can acknowledge uncertainty.

choices.text: Release confirmed information through the authorised spokesperson and correct harmful inaccuracies
choices.feedback: Correct. Timely, verified communication limits misinformation.

steps.situation: Resources are limited and three requests arrive at once.
steps.question: How should they be allocated?

choices.text: Send equal resources to every request
choices.feedback: Equal distribution may ignore very different risk levels.

choices.text: Prioritise by immediate threat to life, cascading risk and operational dependency
choices.feedback: Correct. Risk-based allocation is more defensible than first-come-first-served.

choices.text: Choose the request from the most senior person
choices.feedback: Status should not replace operational risk.

choices.text: Allocate resources according to which request arrived first
choices.feedback: Sequence alone does not reflect threat to life or cascading consequences.

steps.situation: The incident moves into recovery.
steps.question: What should the command team do next?

choices.text: Disband immediately once the public area reopens
choices.feedback: Outstanding risks and staff welfare may remain.

choices.text: Delete temporary logs to avoid confusion
choices.feedback: Logs may be essential for review, learning and accountability.

choices.text: Define recovery ownership, welfare support, evidence retention and a structured debrief
choices.feedback: Correct. Recovery requires governance as well as operational restoration.

choices.text: Return teams to their normal rota and schedule the debrief for a later date
choices.feedback: Recovery needs clear ownership, welfare support, records and a timely structured debrief.

title: Severe Weather Venue Response
description: Balance shelter, evacuation and communication when severe weather threatens a crowded venue.
learningOutcome: Use changing risk information to make coordinated shelter or evacuation decisions.

steps.situation: A severe-weather warning is upgraded while thousands of people are on site.
steps.question: What should leadership do first?

choices.text: Continue normal operations until weather is visible
choices.feedback: Waiting may remove safe options.

choices.text: Announce immediate evacuation before checking routes
choices.feedback: Evacuation may be right, but unsafe routes or timing could worsen risk.

choices.text: Ask each department to decide independently whether to shelter or evacuate
choices.feedback: Fragmented decisions can create conflicting movement and communications.

choices.text: Activate the weather plan, verify timing and assess shelter and exit capacity
choices.feedback: Correct. The decision needs current information and known capacity.

steps.situation: One external route is exposed to high winds.
steps.question: How should this affect the plan?

choices.text: Keep it open to reduce congestion
choices.feedback: Capacity does not justify using an unsafe route.

choices.text: Remove that route from use and direct movement through safer approved options
choices.feedback: Correct. Route safety must be reassessed as conditions change.

choices.text: Let visitors choose whichever route they prefer
choices.feedback: Movement should be coordinated using verified safe routes.

choices.text: Keep the exposed route open for staff only
choices.feedback: The route remains unsafe regardless of who uses it.

steps.situation: Public messages online claim the venue roof is unsafe, but this is unconfirmed.
steps.question: What is the best response?

choices.text: Ignore all public communication
choices.feedback: A vacuum allows misinformation to spread.

choices.text: Confirm the rumour so people leave quickly
choices.feedback: False confirmation can trigger dangerous movement.

choices.text: Issue a verified update, explain the current protective action and monitor official sources
choices.feedback: Correct. Clear facts and instructions reduce rumour-driven movement.

choices.text: Use personal social-media accounts to argue with people sharing the rumour
choices.feedback: Uncoordinated personal replies can amplify misinformation.

steps.situation: Some visitors have mobility needs and the normal assistance team is stretched.
steps.question: What should happen?

choices.text: Prioritise the accessibility plan, allocate support and keep individuals informed
choices.feedback: Correct. Inclusive safety planning must remain active under pressure.

choices.text: Ask companions to manage without support
choices.feedback: Companions may help, but the organisation retains responsibility for its plan.

choices.text: Move everyone at the same speed regardless of need
choices.feedback: This can create harm and block safe movement.

choices.text: Move visitors with mobility needs last so the main crowd can clear first
choices.feedback: Accessibility planning must protect people from being left at greater risk.

steps.situation: Conditions improve after the protective action.
steps.question: What is required before returning to normal?

choices.text: Reopen immediately because the rain has reduced
choices.feedback: Visible improvement may not mean the site is safe.

choices.text: Say nothing and let people move naturally
choices.feedback: Uncontrolled movement can recreate congestion and uncertainty.

choices.text: Stand down some response staff before inspection because conditions appear calmer
choices.feedback: Visible improvement is not a substitute for authorised confirmation and inspection.

choices.text: Receive authorised confirmation, inspect affected areas and communicate a phased stand-down
choices.feedback: Correct. Recovery should be verified and controlled.

title: Critical System Failure During Operations
description: Maintain safe service when a critical digital system fails during peak operations.
learningOutcome: Activate continuity controls, protect data integrity and restore services in a controlled order.

steps.situation: The main operational system becomes unavailable during the busiest period.
steps.question: What is the best immediate response?

choices.text: Declare the incident, switch to the approved continuity process and confirm system scope
choices.feedback: Correct. Structured fallback maintains control while the fault is assessed.

choices.text: Ask staff to invent their own manual processes
choices.feedback: Uncoordinated workarounds create safety and data risks.

choices.text: Restart every server without informing anyone
choices.feedback: Unplanned restarts may worsen the outage and remove evidence.

choices.text: Keep retrying the failed system while teams record informal notes separately
choices.feedback: Repeated retries and fragmented records can worsen disruption and reconciliation.

steps.situation: The manual process is slower and a backlog is growing.
steps.question: How should work be prioritised?

choices.text: Process only the easiest requests
choices.feedback: Ease is not the same as operational importance.

choices.text: Promise normal service to avoid complaints
choices.feedback: False expectations increase pressure and reduce trust.

choices.text: Use agreed criticality rules and communicate realistic service limits
choices.feedback: Correct. Prioritisation protects the most important outcomes.

choices.text: Process requests from senior or VIP users before applying criticality rules
choices.feedback: Priority should be based on operational impact, not status.

steps.situation: Staff are recording data on separate spreadsheets.
steps.question: What control is most important?

choices.text: Let every team design a different sheet
choices.feedback: Different formats make reconciliation unreliable.

choices.text: Use one approved template, clear ownership and a reconciliation plan
choices.feedback: Correct. Controlled records reduce duplication and data loss.

choices.text: Avoid recording anything until the system returns
choices.feedback: Critical actions still need an audit trail.

choices.text: Use timestamped paper records and arrange central reconciliation as soon as possible
choices.feedback: A controlled manual record can support continuity, but one approved process is still preferable.

steps.situation: A vendor says the platform can be restored quickly using an untested patch.
steps.question: What should leadership decide?

choices.text: Apply it immediately to production
choices.feedback: An untested patch may create a larger failure.

choices.text: Reject all vendor support
choices.feedback: Vendor expertise may be valuable when managed safely.

choices.text: Apply the patch to one live server without a rollback plan
choices.feedback: A limited change is still risky without testing, approval and rollback control.

choices.text: Assess risk, test where possible and approve change through emergency governance
choices.feedback: Correct. Urgency should not remove change control entirely.

steps.situation: Service has been restored.
steps.question: What should happen before the incident is closed?

choices.text: Reconcile manual records, confirm stability, document impact and review continuity lessons
choices.feedback: Correct. Recovery includes data accuracy and organisational learning.

choices.text: Delete the manual records because the system is back
choices.feedback: Those records may contain transactions not yet captured.

choices.text: Close the incident as soon as the login screen works
choices.feedback: Technical availability alone does not confirm full operational recovery.

choices.text: Announce full resolution as soon as users can log in, before reconciling the backlog
choices.feedback: Technical access alone does not prove data integrity or operational recovery.
